Yemen is the country in the southwest corner of the Arabian peninsula, with high, green mountains that catch the monsoon rains, a hot coastal plain on the Red Sea, and Aden on the Indian Ocean. On the map it appears from 1000 to 1500, from 1715 to 1815, and from 1920 to now.

In antiquity this was Arabia Felix, the land of Saba and the Himyarites. After Islam, a key line began in 897, when the Zaydi imams, a branch of Shia Islam, set up a state in the northern highlands around Saada. Imams ruled there, with gaps, for over a thousand years, until 1962.

Other dynasties held the south and the coast. The Rasulids, from 1229 to 1454, ruled from Taiz in a golden age of trade, scholarship and farming. The Ottomans came in the 1500s, were driven out by the Zaydi imams by the 1630s, and came back in the 1800s.

Yemen gave the world coffee. Sufis in Yemen took up coffee drinking in the 1400s, and for two centuries the port of Mocha was the world's coffee market.

Modern Yemen was long two states:

  • In the north, the imams' kingdom became fully independent in 1918. A revolution in 1962 started a civil war that ended in a republic.
  • In the south, Britain took Aden in 1839, a coaling port for ships to India; the hinterland became a protectorate. In 1967 it became South Yemen, the Arab world's only Marxist state.

The two united in 1990. Since 2014 the civil war, with Saudi led bombing, has caused one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, including a vast cholera outbreak.
